India’s International Factor Mobility: Roles of Property Rights Protection and Regional Economic Integration

Abstract:

Over the past few decades, the surge in international factor mobility (IFM) in the form of international migration and foreign direct investment (FDI) has received paramount attention in the global economy. It has also been playing a crucial role in shaping economic development by enabling countries to allocate resources more efficiently, facilitating technology transfer, reducing skill shortages, and strengthening economic cooperation. However, its significance for most emerging superpowers like India is unavoidable given their rapid growth and potential economic benefits. The data reveal that India&rsquos IFM, driven by emigration and inward FDI, has increased significantly, leading to an upsurge in the internationalization-led development paradigm of the Indian economy. Over the study period, inward FDI has continued to dominate India&rsquos overall capital inflows and remains a quantitatively and economically more prominent factor. Meanwhile, India is one of the world&rsquos top source countries of emigrants, making the coexistence of substantial capital inflows and labour outflows a defining feature of its international economic participation. Besides, the enhancement of property rights regimes and economic integration plays a major role in reinforcing India&rsquos IFM. Thus, the focus of our study is fourfold. First, to identify the determinants of India&rsquos emigration and inward FDI, and also to investigate their possible substitute or complement relationship. Second, to examine the impact of property rights protection (PRP) on India&rsquos IFM. Third, to investigate the role of regional economic integration (REI) in promoting India&rsquos emigration and inward FDI. Lastly, to explore the joint effects of PRP and REI on India&rsquos IFM. This study uses a panel dataset considering India as the reporting country and 87 partner countries, covering the period from 2000 to 2023. This study applies the augmented gravity model framework and employs estimation techniques like Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood and three-stage least squares.

We find that gravity measures like market size, distance, trade openness, and cultural similarity promote India&rsquos emigration and inward FDI. Additionally, socioeconomic indicators and macroeconomic stability measures significantly influence India&rsquos IFM. Furthermore, although a simultaneous complementary relationship exists between emigration and inward FDI, the interaction term with India&rsquos GDP moderates this relationship, leading to a reversal in the effect&rsquos direction at higher levels of economic development. Similarly, the countries with robust property rights regimes offer better conditions for employment, business creation, and asset accumulation, making them more attractive destinations for Indian migrants. However, when partner countries have significantly stronger property rights regimes than India, foreign firms may perceive a greater institutional disparity, become concerned about the security of their physical and intangible assets, and reduce their investment in the Indian market. Furthermore, both shallow and deep trade agreements (DTAs) promote India&rsquos bilateral emigration and inward FDI, while the effects of DTAs are considerably stronger. Moreover, the joint impact results suggest that DTAs intensify the migration effect associated with differences in PRP between India and its partner countries. In addition, when economic integration between India and partner countries is relatively weak, investors are more sensitive to institutional differences and investment-related risks. Based on the findings, policymakers should place greater emphasis on integrating migration and investment policies to maximize the developmental benefits arising from the complementarities between emigration and inward FDI.

Keywords: IFM, emigration, inward FDI, PRP, REI, India, gravity model, SEM, PPML, 3SLS
